coherence.reason: all six claims answer one question: does the right-to-travel argument let you drive without a licence and walk away from a traffic stop

decision:driving-and-police-stops.question: If I'm only travelling, not driving, do I need a licence, and what happens if I refuse to show one at a stop?
decision:driving-and-police-stops.title: "I'm Not Driving, I'm Travelling": What Courts Actually Say
alternates: Does the right to travel mean you don't need a driver's licence?
What happens when you refuse to show a licence at a traffic stop
decision:driving-and-police-stops.whyWatch: Videos promise that the right words at a traffic stop make a licence optional; the court record shows what those words actually lead to.
decision:driving-and-police-stops.tension: The argument cites real constitutional rights and real court cases, yet the rulings it relies on run the other way.
decision:driving-and-police-stops.evidenceNeeded: A US ruling on whether licensing private drivers is valid police power, the cases the argument cites read in full, and outcomes of stops where drivers refused to identify; a rate of arrests or charges at such stops would settle how common escalation is.
decision:driving-and-police-stops.premise: The right-to-travel argument says a private person travelling in a private car needs no licence and can decline to identify at a stop. The US Supreme Court upheld state licensing and registration of private drivers as police power in Hendrick v. Maryland (1915), and an Ohio appeals court in 2024 rejected the same arguments and noted many courts have; the rulings the argument cites do not hold what it says. The evidence on what happens at the stop is thinner: one Ohio case where refusal ended in removal from the car, arrest and four convictions, and a review describing long standoffs and forcible removals without counting how often stops end in arrest, towing or extra charges.

arc.hook: A driver tells an officer he is travelling, not driving, and refuses to hand over a licence.
arc.conflict: The argument quotes the right to travel and cites court cases; the courts that have ruled on it say driving is a regulable privilege.
arc.evidence: Hendrick v. Maryland upholds licensing of private drivers; State v. Smith rejects the right-to-travel defence and affirms the convictions; the private-use plate and 'not commerce' distinction fails in the same case.
arc.resolution: Licensing and registration are settled law in the cases here, and refusing to identify led to arrest, not release, in the case on record. How often such stops escalate is not measured: the evidence is one case and a review's description, not a rate.
arc.takeaway: The words do not change the law; in the cases on record they added charges.

decision:who-pays-who-profits.question: Who actually comes out ahead when someone uses sovereign-citizen arguments?
decision:who-pays-who-profits.title: Who Really Profits From Sovereign Citizen Seminars?
alternates: The sovereign citizen 'wins': what actually happened
Sovereign citizen gurus get paid. Do their students?
decision:who-pays-who-profits.whyWatch: The pitch is that a paid course or document kit beats the system; the record shows who keeps the money and what happens to the people who use it.
decision:who-pays-who-profits.tension: Teachers point to courtroom wins as proof the theory works, while their students face penalties and convictions.
decision:who-pays-who-profits.evidenceNeeded: Records of what gurus charge, the cases cited as wins read for why the defendant won, and outcomes of litigants who used the arguments; a comparison with similar litigants who argued normally would settle whether they end worse off.
decision:who-pays-who-profits.premise: Government agencies, courts and legal scholars in the US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand describe teachers selling seminars, kits and status services. The cases cited as wins turn out to be decided on ordinary grounds: a jury instruction, an unproved record, a procedural slip. For the students, the sources show added sanctions such as US Tax Court penalties for frivolous positions and describe the litigation as self-destructive, but none compares their outcomes with people in the same position who argued normally, so 'worse off' is the authors' judgment backed by penalties, not a measured comparison.

arc.hook: A seminar promises the secret that makes debts and tickets disappear, for a fee.
arc.conflict: The teachers cite defendants who won; the students who follow them face penalties.
arc.evidence: FBI, Treasury, IRS and court-litigation scholars document the products and prices; the cited wins (Cheek, Porisky, Naudi, a New Zealand acquittal) rest on ordinary legal grounds; frivolous-argument penalties and scholars' accounts show the costs to followers.
arc.resolution: The money flows to the teachers, and the wins were not wins for the theory. Whether followers end worse than if they had argued normally is asserted by experts and supported by added penalties, but no study measures it against a comparison group.
arc.takeaway: When a case is cited as a win, ask what the court actually decided it on.

coherence.reason: every claim is a proposed way out of a court's authority (withheld consent, UCC 1-308, the flag fringe, the 1871 Act, statutes as contracts), and the last asks whether any of them has ever worked

decision:courts-and-jurisdiction.question: Is there anything you can say, sign or point to that takes you out of a court's jurisdiction?
decision:courts-and-jurisdiction.title: The Courtroom Escape Hatches Sovereign Citizens Swear By
alternates: Can you refuse to consent to a court?
UCC 1-308, gold fringe and the 1871 Act: do any of them work?
decision:courts-and-jurisdiction.whyWatch: Each trick is sold as the loophole judges don't want you to know; the rulings on each one show what happens when someone tries it.
decision:courts-and-jurisdiction.tension: The tricks cite real documents (a commercial code section, an 1871 statute, flag law), but what those documents say is not what the tricks claim.
decision:courts-and-jurisdiction.evidenceNeeded: The text of each document the tricks cite, rulings that address each trick, and counts of how such arguments fare across many cases.
decision:courts-and-jurisdiction.premise: Each trick claims a court needs your consent or loses its power by some sign. The documents they cite say otherwise: UCC 1-308 governs reserving rights while performing a commercial contract, the Supreme Court read the 1871 Act as making the District of Columbia a municipal corporation, and a federal court found flag fringe has no legal significance. Courts have rejected the consent and contract arguments in the US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. The strongest evidence that the arguments always fail is Canadian: 1,089 decisions without a success and 51 refused Supreme Court leave applications; a review of 200+ cases across Australia and New Zealand found the same. US evidence is case law and a federal circuit's summary rejection, not a count, so 'uniformly' is shown for Canada and Australasia and stated by US courts rather than tallied.

arc.hook: A defendant writes 'UCC 1-308, without prejudice' under the signature and tells the judge he does not consent.
arc.conflict: Five separate tricks, each pointing to a real document, all aimed at the same thing: a court that has no power over you.
arc.evidence: Read each document for what it says, then the ruling on each trick: Benabe on consent, State v. Smith on 1-308, McCann v. Greenway on the fringe, Metropolitan Railroad on 1871, Bey v. Indiana on statutes as contracts.
arc.resolution: None of the tricks works in any ruling here. The tallies of failure are Canadian and Australasian; in the US the record is a run of rejections, not a count.
arc.takeaway: Jurisdiction comes from law, not from what you sign or say in the room.

decision:money-debt-and-taxes.question: Is there really a secret Treasury account in my name that can pay off my debts?
decision:money-debt-and-taxes.title: The Secret Account Behind Your Birth Certificate
alternates: Can you pay your bills with 'accepted for value'?
Strawman, birth bond, Treasury account: following the redemption story to the end
decision:money-debt-and-taxes.whyWatch: The redemption story promises debts paid from an account you never knew you had; Treasury, the IRS and the courts say what happens to the people who try it.
decision:money-debt-and-taxes.tension: The story links a real document (your birth certificate) to a real agency (the Treasury), so each step sounds checkable, but no step exists.
decision:money-debt-and-taxes.evidenceNeeded: Treasury's and the IRS's own statements on the accounts and instruments, court rulings on strawman, birth-bond and A4V claims, and outcomes for people who used the instruments.
decision:money-debt-and-taxes.premise: The redemption story runs in three steps: the government created a strawman in your all-caps name, sold your birth certificate as a bond, and holds the proceeds in a Treasury account you can draw on by writing 'accepted for value'. Treasury says the account does not exist and the birth certificate has no monetary value; courts in the US, Canada and Australia have called the strawman a myth and the instruments worthless. On the cost, the fraud convictions in the record are of promoters and of people who passed the bills, and a homeowner who paid her mortgage with one lost the house; the sources do not count how often ordinary users are prosecuted, and one cites tax-filing fraud cases rather than debt instruments.

arc.hook: A homeowner sends her bank a $244,663 bill of exchange drawn on her secret Treasury account.
arc.conflict: Each step of the story points to something real, a birth certificate, the Treasury, the commercial code, and promoters sell the kit that ties them together.
arc.evidence: Treasury and the IRS on the account and the instruments; courts on the strawman (Gravatt, Queensland, Canada); Bryant v. Washington Mutual on what the bill of exchange was worth.
arc.resolution: No account, no bond, no strawman: the instruments are worthless in every ruling here. Prosecution is real for promoters and those who passed the bills; how often ordinary users are charged is not measured.
arc.takeaway: If a payment method needs you to believe the Treasury is hiding your money, the bank will treat it as no payment.

decision:status-and-land.question: Can declaring a different status, as a state national, a Moor or a free man, put me outside the law?
decision:status-and-land.title: State Nationals, Moors and Free Men: Can You Declare Yourself Out of the Law?
alternates: Does state national paperwork protect you from police?
Can you opt out of US law by changing your status?
decision:status-and-land.whyWatch: Status paperwork is sold as a way to stop being bound by statutes; the courts that have ruled on each version say what the paperwork does.
decision:status-and-land.tension: Each status borrows something real: the statutory term 'national', old treaties with Morocco, Magna Carta and the common law.
decision:status-and-land.evidenceNeeded: The statute defining US nationals, rulings on Moorish and state-national claims, rulings on common-law and Magna Carta arguments, and records of what happened to people who showed status ID to police; a study of police encounters with such ID would settle the protection claim.
decision:status-and-land.premise: Four versions of one idea: declare a status and the statutes stop applying. By statute 'national of the United States' includes every citizen and confers no exemption; the Seventh Circuit called the Moorish treaty claim baseless; courts in Australia, Canada and Ohio have rejected the argument that common law or Magna Carta overrides statutes. The limits: the federal rulings against 'state citizen' status come from tax cases, so state jurisdiction is not directly tested, and the evidence on status ID at stops is one FBI report that sellers of immunity ID cards were convicted, not a record of what happened to holders at stops.

arc.hook: A driver hands an officer a state-national ID card and says the statutes do not apply to him.
arc.conflict: Each status points to a real source, a statute, a treaty, a charter, and promoters sell the paperwork.
arc.evidence: 8 USC 1101 and USCIS on who is a national; Bey v. Indiana on the Moorish treaty claim; Australian, Canadian and Ohio courts on Magna Carta and common law; federal tax cases on 'state citizen' status; the FBI on immunity ID cards.
arc.resolution: No court here has accepted any of the four. The federal 'state citizen' rulings are tax cases, and the protection-at-stops claim rests on one report about sellers, so those two parts are settled less directly.
arc.takeaway: A status you declare yourself changes nothing a court will recognise.

coherence.reason: one claim, one question: does declaring yourself a state national take you out of the law's reach

conflict:declaring-yourself-american-sta.premise: 'US national' is a real status in federal immigration law, but it describes people owing allegiance to the United States, not people outside its laws. Federal appeals courts have rejected the argument that being a citizen of a state rather than of the United States puts someone beyond federal jurisdiction, in tax cases. The evidence here covers federal jurisdiction in the tax setting; it does not include a ruling on state statutory jurisdiction.

arc.hook: Paperwork sold online promises that declaring yourself an American State National removes you from the system.
arc.resolution: The status in the statute does not mean what the paperwork claims, and federal courts have refused the 'state citizen' escape from federal tax law; the sources here do not test the claim against state law.

coherence.reason: one claim, one question: did leaving gold in 1933 make it impossible to pay a debt

contradicted:since-1933-gold-suspension-.premise: The claim reads the 1933 move off gold as turning money into credit, so debts can only be discharged, never paid. A federal court read the 1933 joint resolution itself and found it makes US currency legal tender for all debts, saying nothing about discharge; Congress declares Federal Reserve Notes legal tender, and federal circuits reject as frivolous the claim that they are merely debts.
